L7: ## What we do
L8: 
L9: CASTR Alliance aims to advance human and veterinary medicine by facilitating the discovery of innovative treatments through the management of high-quality veterinary clinical studies and collaboration with industry leaders and veterinary hospitals.
L10: 
L11: We provide turnkey management of sponsored veterinary clinical studies to pharmaceutical and medical device development teams worldwide.
L12: We partner with state-of-the-art veterinary specialty and referral hospitals throughout the Pacific Northwest and beyond to enroll patients on sponsored clinical studies.
L13: 
L14: We manage sponsored clinical trials that abide by Good Clinical Practice (GCP) standards for veterinary studies and are designed to ensure the collection of high-quality data.
L15: We submit all CASTR-run studies for ethical review by an external Veterinary Clinical Studies Committee (VCSC) to prioritize the safety and well-being of all patients.
L16: 
L17: 【4†MORE DETAILS】
L18: ## What motivates us
L19: 
L20: The motivations behind CASTR Alliance’s efforts are to connect companion animals with cutting-edge treatments, address naturally occurring diseases in pets, and accelerate medical innovation for both animals and humans through clinical trials.
L21: 
L22: #### Linking Patients to Caregivers
L23: 
L24: Our sponsored studies link companion animals in need of innovative solutions to novel therapeutic or diagnostic options that may otherwise be unavailable to them.
L25: #### Studying Spontaneous Diseases
L26: 
L27: Our research focuses on spontaneous diseases – those that arise naturally in dogs and cats. By enrolling companion animals who are already afflicted or symptomatic, we aim to provide potential direct benefits to our pets while gathering data that could help human or animal patients in the future.
L28: 
L29: #### Accelerating Medical Innovation
L30: 
L31: When a pet is enrolled in a CASTR-managed clinical trial, they take part in helping advance medical discovery and innovation.
L32: ## 【5†Translational research:】 Caring for our pets while advancing human and animal healthcare
L33: 
L34: ## What to expect
L35: 
L36: #### Contracting companies
L37: 
L38: can expect all CASTR Alliance-run studies to be managed efficiently and ethically, adhere to GCP standards, and result in high quality data. We deliver progress updates upon request throughout the trial, conduct diligent site and safety monitoring, and provide data at interim analysis, and at the conclusion of the trial.
L39: #### Veterinary clinicians
L40: 
L41: and support staff participating in the study are trained from the onset on the trial protocol to ensure treatment is conducted according to our rigorous standards. We continue to provide guidance and support to our participating sites throughout the entire course of the study.
L42: #### Pet owners
L43: 
L44: who enroll their pets in these clinical studies engage directly with a participating veterinary center, where all study procedures are carried out in accordance with the established study protocol. Studies are typically supported such that treatment is partially or fully covered by the sponsor.
L45: ## WHO WE ARE
L46: CASTR Alliance was founded in 2019 by veterinary clinician-scientists Jessica Bertout and Jim Perry. As scientists, they bring extensive experience in designing, managing, and conducting clinical trials that meet the rigorous standards of the biotech industry. Moreover, as devoted pet owners and veterinarians, they are personally committed to delivering the highest quality care for our animal companions. Together, Drs.
L47: Bertout and Perry created CASTR Alliance to leverage their expertise and advance medicine for humans and animals alike.

L76: ### 治験・臨床試験情報案内
L77: 
L78: #### 犬のリンパ系腫瘍に対する抗CD20抗体による臨床試験
L79: 
L80:   * 犬のリンパ系腫瘍（リンパ腫、白血病など）に対する新規治療法として、抗CD20抗体による臨床試験を行っております。
L81:   * この治療法は、通常の抗がん剤治療とは異なり、分子標的療法に分類されます。
L82: 抗CD20抗体は、医療ではリツキサン®という名前の薬剤が1998年よりすでに使用されており、リンパ腫などの患者さんに対して多大な貢献をしている薬ですが、これを【30†我々の研究室において†www.mizutakuvet.com】犬用に独自に開発した同様の薬剤です。
L83:   * 対象となる腫瘍、試験内容などについての条件がございますので、ご興味ある方は水野（mizutaku@yamaguchi-u.ac.jp）までご一報いただきますよう宜しくお願い致します。
L84: #### 犬の免疫介在性疾患に対する他家脂肪由来幹細胞による臨床試験
L85: 
L86:   * 犬のさまざまな難治性免疫介在性疾患に対する新規治療法として、他家脂肪由来幹細胞を用いた臨床試験を行っております。
L87:   * この治療法は、再生医療に分類される新しい治療法で、脂肪由来幹細胞によって免疫調節することを目的としております。アニコム先進医療研究所株式会社（【31†https://www.anicom.co.jp†www.anicom.co.jp】）との共同で行っております。
L88:   * 対象となる疾患、試験内容などについての条件がございますので、ご興味ある方は水野（mizutaku@yamaguchi-u.ac.jp）までご一報いただきますよう宜しくお願い致します。
L89: #### 犬の腫瘍（がん）の早期診断に関する臨床研究
L90: 
L91:   * 犬の様々な腫瘍（がん）を早期に検出すること、また、再発を予測することを目的とした臨床研究を行っています。
L92:   * 研究にご提供いただくものは血液のみであり、実現すれば動物へのダメージを最小限に抑えた腫瘍検査を行うことができるようになると期待されます。
L93:   * 対象となるのは腫瘍性疾患または感染・炎症性疾患の犬です。貧血または3kgを下回る体重の犬は、採血の影響を考慮して研究対象外としています。
L94:   * その他、本研究のより詳しい情報についてのお問い合わせは上林（s-kam@yamaguchi-u.ac.jp）までご連絡ください。
L95: #### 犬の腫瘍（がん）に対する免疫チェックポイント分子（PD-1）阻害抗体による臨床試験
L96: 
L97:   * 犬の様々な腫瘍（がん）に対する新規治療法として、免疫チェックポイント分子（PD-1）阻害抗体による臨床試験を行っております。
L98:   * これまでの外科治療、抗がん剤治療、放射線治療とは全く異なる新しい治療法であり、分子標的療法に分類されます。抗PD-1抗体は、医療ではオプジーボ®、キートルーダ®という名前の薬剤としてがん治療に用いられていますが、【30†我々の研究室において†www.mizutakuvet.com】犬用に独自開発した同様の薬剤を用います。

L20: # Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer
L21: 
L22: Links last verified: August 20, 2026
L23: ## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology
L24: 
L25: When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.
L26: 
L27: Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.
L28: 
L29: These may include:
L30:   * A dog’s breed
L31:   * Age
L32:   * Weight
L33:   * Overall health
L34:   * Life expectancy
L35:   * Cancer type
L36:   * Cancer stage
L37:   * Previous care
L38:   * ...and other medical factors
L39: 
L40: Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.
L41: 
L42: It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.
L43: Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments. Families may still be responsible for additional veterinary expenses, travel, lodging, and repeated visits over several weeks or months, especially when a study is located far from home.
L44: 
L45: The following links are intended to help pet parents and veterinary professionals find information about current canine oncology trials being conducted throughout the United States and, in some cases, internationally.
L46: We encourage families to carefully review each study’s eligibility requirements, location, potential costs, time commitment, and possible benefits and risks with their veterinary team.
L47:

L51: ## Start Here: Nationwide Search Tools
L52: 
L53: If you are not sure where to begin, start with the AVMA registry. It lets you search by cancer type and by location, which is faster than checking individual centers one at a time.
L54: #### 【65†AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry†veterinaryclinicaltrials.org】
L55: 
L56: The AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry, formerly known as the AVMA Animal Health Studies Database, helps dog parents and veterinary professionals find veterinary clinical studies taking place throughout the United States and Canada. By making this information easier to access, the registry supports continued research and progress in veterinary medicine and canine health care.
L57: If you are interested in a clinical trial for your dog, begin by discussing the study and your dog’s potential eligibility with your veterinary care provider.
L58: 
L59: 
L60: 
L61: 【65†AVMA Clinical Trials†veterinaryclinicaltrials.org】
L62: #### 【67†National Cancer Institute, Comparative Oncology Program†ccr.cancer.gov】
L63: 
L64: The Comparative Oncology Program develops and conducts clinical trials in partnership with veterinary teaching institutions throughout the United States. Dogs enrolled in these studies receive care from board-certified veterinary oncologists committed to improving comfort, quality of life, and cancer care for companion animals.
L65: The knowledge gained through this research may help advance the understanding of cancer and support future progress in both canine and human oncology.
L66:

L68: #### 【68†PetCure Oncology†petcureoncology.com】
L69: 
L70: PetCure Oncology provides stereotactic radiation surgery and stereotactic radiation therapy, commonly known as SRS and SRT. These highly precise forms of radiation therapy have been used in human oncology and are now available for dogs with certain types of cancer.
L71: PetCure Oncology reports using SRS and SRT in thousands of companion animals with a variety of tumor types. Its affiliated veterinary specialists continue to study these approaches to better understand their potential benefits, safety considerations, side effects, and appropriate applications in canine cancer care.

L30: ## Why enroll your dog in a clinical trial?
L31: 
L32: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor of dogs. Nearly 10,000 dogs are diagnosed with this cancer each year.  The incidence of 【8†osteosarcoma in dogs†www.csuanimalcancercenter.org】 is anywhere from 10-50x higher than in humans.  Research in dogs will one day mean better treatment for kids.
L33: Enrolling a dog in a clinical trial can offer several potential benefits to both the individual pet and the broader veterinary community. Here are some reasons why pet owners may consider enrolling their dogs in clinical trials:
L34:   * Access to Cutting-Edge Treatments: Clinical trials often investigate novel treatments, therapies, or medications that are not yet available to the general public. By participating in a clinical trial, pet owners may gain access to potentially more effective or advanced treatments for their dog's condition.
L35:   * Contributing to Scientific Knowledge: Clinical trials are essential for advancing veterinary medicine. By participating, pet owners help researchers gather data and evidence that can lead to new understandings of diseases, improved treatments, and better overall care for animals in the future.
L36:   * Expert Monitoring and Care: Dogs enrolled in clinical trials receive close monitoring and care from experienced veterinarians and researchers. This regular attention can be beneficial in managing the dog's health and detecting any changes or side effects early on.
L37:   * Potential Cost Savings: In some cases, the cost of participating in a clinical trial may be partially or fully covered by the sponsoring organization. This can ease the financial burden on pet owners, especially when dealing with expensive medical treatments.
L38: 
L39:   * Supportive Community: Pet owners in clinical trials become part of a supportive community of other caregivers and veterinary professionals who are invested in finding solutions and improving the health outcomes for animals.
L40:   * Personal Satisfaction: Knowing that they are actively contributing to the advancement of veterinary medicine and potentially helping other animals in the future can be personally rewarding for pet owners.
L41: Before enrolling a dog in a clinical trial, it's crucial for pet owners to thoroughly understand the study's purpose, potential risks, and benefits. They should also discuss the decision with their primary veterinarian to ensure it aligns with their dog's specific health needs and well-being. Clinical trials typically have specific inclusion and exclusion criteria, so not all dogs will be eligible for every study.
L42: Therefore, it's essential to work closely with the research team to determine the most suitable options for the dog's condition.

L72: # CICV – Centre d’investigation clinique vétérinaire
L73: ## Le CICV et la recherche clinique
L74: 
L75: Implanté au sein du 【8†Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Vétérinaire de VetAgro Sup】, le CICV met ses moyens humains et matériels au service de toutes les spécialités vétérinaires (un devis peut-être obtenu sur simple demande).
L76: Il veille à la sécurité des animaux et au respect des BPCv. Le CICV optimise la coordination des études, le respect du protocole et les procédures pour garantir la qualité des données recueillies.
L77: La recherche clinique comprend l’ensemble des études scientifiques réalisées sur un animal, présenté en consultation auprès d’un vétérinaire. Elle concerne l’animal sain ou malade dit « de compagnie » ou « de rente » appartenant à une personne physique ou morale mais également l’animal sauvage ; elle se distingue ainsi clairement de l’expérimentation animale (animal de laboratoire).
L78: La recherche clinique vétérinaire a pour objectif premier d’améliorer la santé animale en produisant, à partir de situations cliniques, de nouvelles connaissances en matière épidémiologique, étiologique et pathogénique, physiopathologique, thérapeutique et prophylactique, sans oublier les considérations médico-économiques et les aspects humains et sociaux.
L79: Ces recherches, réalisées dans le respect de la législation et de l’éthique, sont indispensables pour mieux comprendre, traiter et prévenir les maladies animales.

L126: ### Structure d’appui unique
L127: 
L128: Les meilleurs centres médicaux n’appliquent pas seulement les connaissances les plus récentes, ils les créent. Le CICV de VetAgro Sup travaille en partenariat avec les professionnels du secteur de la santé, des cliniciens, des chercheurs académiques et des industriels.
L129: 
L130: Le CICV réalise des études conformes aux réglementations des bonnes pratiques cliniques vétérinaires (BPCv) et des bonnes pratiques de laboratoire (BPL).
L131: Le rôle du CICV de VetAgro Sup est avant tout d’apporter un soutien méthodologique réglementaire et logistique nécessaire aux demandeurs. Il développe et facilite ainsi les études cliniques vétérinaires qui peuvent conduire à de nouveaux traitements, médicaments, procédures et dispositifs médicaux.
L132: En collaboration avec les services de formation de VetAgro Sup, le centre favorise également la formation professionnelle, notamment aux bonnes pratiques cliniques vétérinaires et encourage l’accueil de stagiaires.
L133: ## Accompagnement sur mesure
L134: 
L135: L’aide apportée par le CICV s’adapte aux besoins des demandeurs publics ou privés. Une évaluation personnalisée des besoins est réalisée pour chaque demande.
L136: 
L137: Si VetAgro Sup est « promoteur »
L138: 
L139: Le CICV de VetAgro Sup peut contribuer :
L140:   * Au montage des protocoles (élaboration du protocole, du résumé, de la notice d’information, des consentements, des procédures d’investigation)
L141:   * À l’estimation des coûts et à la recherche de financements (réponse aux appels à projet)
L142:   * À la mise en place des études cliniques dans les centres participants et à leur coordination
L143: 
L144: Si VetAgro Sup est « centre associé »
L145: 
L146: Le CICV de VetAgro Sup peut réaliser et organiser :
L147:   * Les visites de sélection menées par le promoteur
L148:   * L’identification de l’équipe projet impliquée
L149:   * La mise en place et le suivi de l’étude (inclusion des sujets sains ou malades, amendement, prélèvement, monitoring, gestion des évènements indésirables)
L150:   * La clôture et archivage de l’étude

L20: ## Kv9 Pilot Study
L21: 
L22: Purpose of study:
L23: 
L24: To assess efficacy and safety of Kv9 across a range of solid tumours.
L25: 
L26: ​
L27: 
L28: Eligible tumour types:
L29: 
L30:   * Soft tissue sarcomas
L31: 
L32:   * Mast cell tumours
L33: 
L34:   * Mammary gland tumours
L35: 
L36:   * Melanomas
L37: 
L38:   * Anal gland tumours
L39: 
L40:   * Squamous cell carcinomas
L41: 
L42:   * Other tumours may be considered
L43: 
L44: ​
L45: 
L46: Primary eligibility criteria*: ​
L47: 
L48:   * Tumour type diagnosed by fine needle aspirate or biopsy by a registered veterinary pathologist
L49: 
L50:   * ​Tumour smaller than 5cm
L51:   * Not receiving immune modulatory drugs
L52: 
L53:     * It is acceptable to be taking/receiving including apoquel, cytopoint, beranza or a recent vaccination
L54: 
L55:   * No wounds on the surface of soft tissue sarcoma tumours
L56: 
L57:     * Other tumour types will be a case by case basis ​
L58: 
L59: *See referral form for complete criteria ​
L60: 
L61: ​​​
L62: 
L63: Study protocol:
L64: 
L65:   1. Primary veterinarian to send through referral for assessment by Kode Veterinary Sciences (KVS).

L6: # Clinical Study for Cats with Mammary Cancer - Information for referring veterinarians
L7: 
L8: ##
L9: ## Why refer your patients?
L10: 
L11:   * The therapy (GCN2-IN-6) has been carefully tested in preclinical studies and is well-tolerated.
L12:   * Your referred patients will receive standard surgical care plus the investigational therapy.
L13:   * Participation contributes valuable data for advancing cancer treatments in both cats and humans.
L14: ## Study design highlights
L15: 
L16:   * Neo-adjuvant and adjuvant therapy administered around the time of mastectomy.
L17: 
L18:   * Safety and efficacy are continuously monitored.
L19: 
L20:   * Feline mammary adenocarcinoma is a validated model for TNBC research.
L21: ## Referral process
L22: 
L23:   * Eligible cats: cats diagnosed with mammary tumors, eligible for surgery.
L24: 
L25:   * As referring veterinarians, you can retain primary responsibility for routine care; the study team coordinates treatment administration and follow-up.
L26: 
L27:   * Participation is voluntary, and owners can withdraw at any time.
L28: ## Impact:
L29: 
L30: By referring cats to this study, you are helping advance cutting-edge cancer research, improve therapeutic options, and potentially enhance outcomes for both feline and human patients.
L31: ## Contact
L32: 
L33: Further information can be obtained by mailing Ada Krupa (adriana.krupa@ugent.be) or Hilde de Rooster (hilde.derooster@ugent.be) or by phone (+32 9 264 77 00).

L6: # Clinical Study for Cats with Mammary Cancer - Information for owners
L7: 
L8: ##
L9: 
L10: ## The care your cat will receive
L11: ### Standard surgical care
L12: 
L13: Your cat will undergo routine tumour removal, just like any cat receiving mammary gland surgery at our Veterinary Teaching Hospital.
L14: 
L15: ### Innovative therapy
L16: 
L17: In addition to standard treatment, your cat will receive the investigational therapy (GCN2-IN-6) that will need to be administered orally before and after the surgery.
L18: ### Close monitoring
L19: 
L20: Apart from you as an owner, veterinary specialists will follow your cat throughout the study to ensure their comfort, safety, and well-being.
L21: Preclinical studies at the Small Animal Department demonstrated that this therapy is well-tolerated by cats, with little to no side effects nor with any relevant changes in any blood parameter.
L22: 
L23: ## Benefits and Impact
L24: ### Potential benefit for your cat
L25: 
L26: Participation may help to lower the risk of tumour recurrence and/or tumour spread (metastasis).
L27: The novel drug will be supplied without any additional cost.
L28: 
L29: ### Advancing feline care
L30: 
L31: Your cat’s involvement contributes valuable information toward developing new cancer treatments to increase the life expectancy for cats.
L32: ### Helping humans too
L33: 
L34: The insights gained from this study in cats could pave the way to initiate clinical trials in people with aggressive breast cancers, including TNBC.
L35: 
L36: ## Your Contribution Makes a Difference
L37: 
L38: Without caring owners like you, advancing new treatments to improve the health and lifespan of pets wouldn’t be possible. By participating, you are making a meaningful contribution to advancements in veterinary medicine and helping shape better care for cats, today and in the future.
L39: ### Voluntary participation
L40: 
L41: Participation in this clinical study is completely voluntary. In consultation with the responsible researchers, you may withdraw your cat at any time, without affecting future veterinary care.
L42: 
L43: ### Where the study takes place
L44: 
L45: The study will be conducted at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital of Ghent University, Salisburylaan 133, B-9820 Merelbeke-Melle.
L46: ### Contact information
L47: 
L48: For further information concerning this study, please do not hesitate to contact veterinarian A. Krupa  (adriana.krupa@ugent.be) or Prof. H. de Rooster (hilde.derooster@ugent.be) or contact the reception of the Veterinary Teaching Hospital (+32 9 264 77 00).

L72: # Etude pour développer un nouveau médicament pour traiter les mélanomes et carcinomes épidermoïdes buccaux.
L73: ## Votre chien est atteint d’une tumeur orale maligne ?
L74: 
L75: L’équipe de Cancérologie de VetAgro Sup et le Centre d’Investigation Clinique Vétérinaire (CICV) mènent actuellement une étude en collaboration avec la société biopharmaceutique FINDIMMUNE, qui développe des thérapies anticancéreuses et immunitaires, afin de développer un nouveau médicament pour traiter les mélanomes et carcinomes épidermoïdes buccaux.
L76: ### Détails de l'étude
L77: 
L78: L’étude consiste en l’administration intra-tumorale du médicament innovant.
L79: 
L80: Cette recherche implique 10 visites sur le site de VetAgro Sup sur une durée de 6 mois.
L81: 
L82: Une première visite de sélection est prévue au service de Cancérologie pour confirmer le diagnostic de votre chien.
L83: 
L84: Le traitement prévoit 3 injections programmées à J1, J30 et J90, ainsi que des visites de suivi à J7, J15, J60, J120, J150 et J180.
L85: Votre chien aura accès gratuitement au traitement innovant et son suivi médical sera entièrement pris en charge.
L86: 
L87: A ce jour, il n’existe pas d’alternative médicamenteuse pour le traitement des tumeurs orales malignes. La participation de votre chien à cette étude ouvrira la voie à un nouveau traitement des mélanomes et carcinomes chez le chien. Cela améliorera considérablement la qualité de vie des chiens traités.
L88: Si vous souhaitez participer, n’hésitez pas à contacter le secrétariat des cliniques afin de prendre rendez-vous en Cancérologie au 0478872670 En cas de question sur cette étude, vous pouvez contacter le CICV : cicv@vetagro-sup.fr
L89: 
L90: Nous vous remercions par avance de l’aide que vous pourrez nous apporter et de votre contribution.

L6: 
L7: NL
L8: 
L9: Heeft uw hond een carcinoom (bv. plaveiselcelcarcinoom, adenocarcinoom, mammacarcinoom...) die voor chirurgie in aanmerking komt en wil u meewerken aan wetenschappelijk onderzoek?
L10: 
L11: De behandeling gaat door in de Universitaire Dierenkliniek Kleine Huisdieren van de Universiteit Gent.
L12: 
L13: 
L14: 
L15: Procedure:
L16: - Ofwel wordt de Nanobody-kleurstof vlak voor de operatie ingespoten, ofwel wordt de Nanobody-kleurstof na chirurgische wegname van de kanker op het wondbed gesprayed.
L17: 
L18: - De verdoving zal dezelfde zijn als bij honden die chirurgie ondergaan en niet aan het onderzoek deelnemen.
L19: 
L20: - De chirurgische benadering zal dezelfde zijn als bij honden die niet aan het onderzoek deelnemen.
L21: - Het operatienveld zal met een speciale camera worden belicht. Op een beeldscherm zal dan duidelijk worden waar de kankercellen zich bevinden omdat ze zullen oplichten (fluoresceren).
L22: 
L23: - Nadat het tumoraal weefsel werd verwijderd, zal het wondbed opnieuw worden bekeken met de speciale camera en zullen eventuele resterende fluorescerende cellen worden verwijderd.
L24: Zonder eigenaren zoals u is het onmogelijk om nieuwe behandelingen te ontwikkelen die het welzijn maar ook de levensverwachting van uw viervoeter verbeteren. Wij stellen uw bijdrage aan de vooruitgang van de diergeneeskunde ten zeerste op prijs. Deelname aan dit onderzoek zal ook helpen om deze toepassing tijdens chirurgie bij mensen verder te verbeteren.
L25: Deelname aan deze klinische studie verloopt op vrijwillige basis. Vooraleer uw hond aan de klinische studie kan deelnemen, moet u een schriftelijke verklaring ondertekenen. Als dank voor uw medewerking bieden we u het histologisch onderzoek en de eerste consultatie gratis aan.
L26: 
L27: 
L28: 
L29: Voor meer informatie en voor doorverwijzing kan contact opgenomen worden met dierenarts Nayra Valle via nayra.valle@ugent.be of Professor Hilde de Rooster (Weke Delen Chirurgie) via hilde.derooster@ugent.be.
L30: 
L31: 
L32: 
L33: EN
L34: Does your dog have a carcinoma (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, mammary carcinoma...) eligible for surgery and would you like to participate in scientific research?
L35: 
L36: Treatment goes on at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital of Ghent University.
L37: 
L38: 
L39: 
L40: Procedure:
L41: 
L42: - Either the compound will be injected just before surgery, or it will be sprayed on the wound bed after surgical removal of the cancer.
L43: 
L44: - Anesthesia will be the same as in dogs undergoing surgery and not participating in the study.
L45: - The surgical approach will be the same as in dogs not participating in the study.
L46: 
L47: - The surgical field will be imaged with a special camera. A screen will then show where the cancer cells are since they will light up (fluoresce).
L48: 
L49: - After the tumor tissue has been removed, the wound bed will be imaged again with the camera and any remaining fluorescent cells (possibly cancerous) will be removed.
L50: Without owners like you, it is impossible to develop new treatments that improve the well-being and the life expectancy of your four-legged friend. We greatly appreciate your contribution to the advancement of veterinary medicine. Participation in this study will also help to further accelerate the application of this technique during surgery in humans.
L51: Participation in this clinical trial is voluntary. Before your dog can participate in the clinical trial, you must sign an informed consent statement. As a token of appreciation for your cooperation, we offer the histological examination and initial consultation free of charge.
L52: 
L53: 
L54: 
L55: For more information and/or referral, please contact veterinarian Nayra Valle at nayra.valle@ugent.be  or Professor Hilde de Rooster (Soft Tissue Surgery) at hilde.derooster@ugent.be.

L41: Species: Dog
L42: 
L43: Area of Study: Medical Oncology
L44: Purpose of Study: The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL.
L45: 
L46: In this study, your dog will be randomly selected to receive either CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. At each visit, their lymph node size, blood work, and overall wellbeing will be assessed.
L47: Timeline: Both protocols involve treatments every 7–14 days and take 4-6 months to complete. Following protocol completion, your pet will return once monthly to assess remission status.
L48: 
L49: Eligibility: Your dog may qualify if:
L50:   * Confirmed peripheral T cell lymphoma diagnosis via cytology or histopathology
L51:     * No indolent forms of lymphoma, such as T zone lymphoma
L52:     * Cutaneous lymphoma will not be included
L53:   * No prior chemotherapy or radiation therapy for lymphoma. It is preferred that patients are not started on steroids in advance of enrollment. However, if deemed by the overseeing clinician, patients can still be enrolled on steroids for up to 10 days.
L54:   * No major lab work abnormalities that prevent chemotherapy administration
L55:   * No evidence of dilated cardiomyopathy, ventricular arrhythmia, or liver failure
L56: ## T Cell Diagnostic Testing
L57: 
L58: A diagnosis of T cell lymphoma can be made using one or more of the following tests:
L59: 
L60:   * Immunocytochemistry (ICC)*
L61:   * Immunohistochemistry (IHC)*
L62:   * PCR for antigen receptor rearrangements (PARR)*
L63:   * Flow cytometry
L64: 
L65: *Available through the 【12†MSU Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory†vdl.msu.edu】
L66: 
L67: Client Benefits: This is a partially funded trial.
L68:   * A test must be conducted to confirm the T cell lymphoma diagnosis in study participants. T cell diagnostic testing can be conducted at MSU or through clients’ primary care veterinarians. Diagnostic testing at MSU costs approximately $250. For dogs accepted to the study, the cost will be reimbursed by an account credit at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center at trial completion (either when the protocol is completed or the patient develops progressive disease).
L69:   * Initial evaluation appointments will be charged. For dogs accepted to the study, recheck exams during clinical trial appointments will be free of cost ($60 value per visit). Costs associated with blood work and treatment will remain the responsibility of the client (with the exception described below).
L70:   * Dogs will receive the first dose of doxorubicin (for those assigned to the CHOP protocol) or lomustine (for those assigned to the LOPP protocol) free of cost. First-dose administrative and blood work fees also will be free of cost.
L71:   * Clients are financially responsible for all treatments and diagnostics that are unrelated to the study.
L72: Client Responsibilities:
L73:   * To administer prednisone, chemotherapy, or supplemental medications as prescribed by the attending veterinarian.
L74:   * To comply with the visit schedule outlined by study investigators
L75:   * To report any abnormal behavior or signs of illness to study investigators.
L76:   * To contact study investigators if your dog is evaluated by any other veterinarians during the course of the study.
L77:   * To inform study investigators of any non-study-related veterinary treatments recommended for your dog during the course of the study.
L78: Contact Information: Please feel free to contact our Medical Oncology Team at (517) 353-5420 or cvm.oncoinfo@msu.edu to refer a patient or for any additional information. Referring veterinarian and client calls are welcome.

L54: 
L55: Purpose of the study:
L56: Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive cancer in dogs that often does not respond well to standard treatments like chemotherapy or radiation. While some dogs experience benefits, these treatments affect many cells at once and cannot adapt as a tumor changes. New research shows that cancer closely interacts with the immune system and surrounding tissues, suggesting that better treatments may need to work inside cells, not just target them from the outside.
L57: Quasiorganelle therapy is an experimental approach that aims to do this by using weakened, non-disease-causing bacteria derived from Listeria monocytogenes to deliver helpful genetic instructions directly into immune and tumor cells, with the goal of improving how the body recognizes and responds to cancer.
L58: The aim of this study is to determine whether quasiorganelle therapy can be given safely to dogs with histiocytic sarcoma and to determine an appropriate dosing schedule. The treatment has been tested in laboratory and preclinical studies but not yet in dogs with naturally-occurring cancer. Because animals with cancer may respond differently than healthy animals, this study also looks for early biological or clinical signs that the therapy may be beneficial.
L59: 
L60: Inclusion criteria:
L61:   * Confirmed diagnosis of histiocytic sarcoma, including hemophagocytic histiocytic sarcoma, as determined by immune marker expression.
L62:   * Visible tumor at the time of enrollment.
L63:     * Up to 5 lesions
L64:     * Sum of the longest lesion dimensions <15cm
L65:   * Adequate organ function indicated by standard laboratory tests.
L66:   * Minimum weight requirement of 20 kg (44 lbs).
L67:   * VCOG performance status up to 2.
L68: 
L69: Exclusion criteria:
L70:   * Concurrent diseases such as: diabetes mellitus, Addison’s disease (hypoadrenocorticism), Cushing’s disease (hyperadrenocorticism), kidney disease
L71:   * Active wounds.
L72:   * Concurrent medications such as: immunosuppressants (including corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine, mycophenolate) or systemic antibiotics within 14 days.
L73:   * Neutropenia, immunodeficiency, or immune-mediated disease
L74:   * Prior anti-cancer treatment
L75:     * Corticosteroid (prednisone) within 7 days.
L76:     * Chemotherapy within 14 days.
L77:     * Radiation therapy within 30 days.
L78: Treatment:
L79: The first group (8 dogs) will receive quasiorganelle therapy alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the quasiorganelle infusion. They will then be observed for up 4 days at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center and blood and fecal samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return for treatment once weekly for 4 doses followed by 2 weeks off. This schedule will then be repeated two more times for a total of 16 weeks of treatment.
L80: Imaging to determine alterations in tumor size will be repeated at the end of each 4 week treatment period.
L81: The second group (8 dogs) will receive quaisorganelle therapy that includes gene therapy. Their treatment and monitoring schedule will be identical to that of the first group.
L82: 
L83: Following the 16 week treatment period, dogs will return for evaluation every 4 weeks or until progressive disease is documented.
L84: 
L85: Please note: While enrolled, dogs should not live with anyone who is pregnant or planning to become pregnant.
L86: 
L87: Compensation:
L88:   * This is a funded trial. All tests and treatments associated with the trial will be covered once a dog is enrolled.
L89:   * Complications associated with the trial will be covered. Clients are financially responsible for all treatments and diagnostics that are unrelated to the trial. Association between complications and trial treatment will be determined by the overseeing clinician and investigators.
L90:   * Initial evaluation appointments will be charged.
L91:   * Quasiorganelle therapy (with or without gene therapy) will be administered free of cost. Hospitalization immediately following administration and associated treatments will be free of cost. Blood and fecal sampling and imaging studies associated with the trial will be free of cost.
L92: Contact information: Please feel free to contact our Medical Oncology Team at (517) 353-5420 or cvm.oncoinfo@msu.edu to refer a patient or for any additional information. Referring veterinarian and client calls are welcome.

L53: Clinical Study: Time to Maximal Response to Neoadjuvant Corticosteroids in Dogs with Mast Cell Tumors
L54: 
L55: Purpose of Study:
L56: Mast cell tumors (MCT) are the most common skin tumor in dogs. MCTs can be treated in a variety of ways, with surgery being a common component of care. When MCTs are located in a challenging surgical location, we will try pre-treating with drugs to shrink the tumor and give the surgeon more flexibility. Historically, these pre-surgical treatments include chemotherapy and/or corticosteroids. Anecdotally, if the MCT shrinks, the effect only lasts for a limited period.
L57: To date, there are no studies identifying the ideal time between starting steroids and performing surgery. In this study, we plan to identify canine patients with cutaneous MCTs, administer corticosteroids, and before proceeding to surgery, clients (pet owners) will obtain daily measurements.
L58: The aim of this study is to identify guidelines for pre-operative steroid treatment with secondary goals of decreasing surgical risks and improving post-operative outcomes in dogs affected by this disease. Identifying an ideal pre-surgical treatment window can improve veterinarian confidence in surgical scheduling, help facilitate successful surgery, and limit the influence of steroids on wound healing.
L59: 
L60: Eligibility Criteria:
L61:   * Inclusion criteria:
L62:     * Confirmed mast cell tumor diagnosis via cytology or histopathology (may be completed through primary veterinarian or at MSU)
L63:     * Cutaneous mast cell tumor located on the trunk (above the elbow or knee)
L64:     * Mast cell tumor measures between 2-6cm in one dimension
L65:     * Bloodwork confirming adequate organ function and ability to undergo general anesthesia (may be completed through primary veterinarian or at MSU)
L66:   * Exclusion criteria:
L67:     * Prior anti-cancer treatment, including steroids, within 7 days
L68:     * Patients on NSAIDs need 5 or more days of washout before enrolling
L69:     * Evidence of MCT metastasis
L70:     * Expected survival < 4 weeks with treatment
L71:     * Diabetes mellitus or other systemic condition that interferes with safe steroid administration
L72: Eligibility Diagnostics:
L73: 
L74: Prior to study entry, pet owners will be responsible for an initial consultation at MSU and to complete the following diagnostics for their dog:
L75: 
L76:   * Cytology or histopathology of tumor in question to confirm diagnosis of MCT (if not already completed)
L77:   * Bloodwork ensuring adequate organ function to undergo general anesthesia (if not already completed)
L78: Staging diagnostics including abdominal ultrasound with cytologic evaluation of regional lymph nodes, spleen, and/or liver will be contingent on a overseeing clinician’s recommendation as well as client election. This is not a requirement for inclusion.
L79: 
L80: Treatment:
L81: Initial caliper measurements of the tumor will be obtained by 2 trained staff members on the day of enrollment. Clients will be trained by MSU staff in caliper usage and each dog will be prescribed prednisone, diphenhydramine, and either famotidine or omeprazole for 14 days.
L82: Each morning, the clients will obtain caliper measurements of the MCT in the 3 planes as instructed per specific training images. Photographs that include the caliper will be emailed to the primary investigators daily. In-person evaluations will be completed at MSU on days 7 and 14 to confirm measurement accuracy and allow for surgical planning.
L83: Surgical resection will be planned for Day 14 (+/- 1 day) with the MSU Soft Tissue Surgery service, and tissue will be submitted for biopsy analysis. Patients who experience significant or rapid tumor shrinkage may undergo surgery sooner.
L84: 
L85: If at any time throughout treatment, the tumor grows by >20%, the patient will be removed from the trial and given appropriate care based on clinician discretion.
L86: 
L87: Compensation:
L88:   * This is a partially funded trial
L89:     * Up to 50% of the surgical fees and the histopathology fees will be covered
L90:     * All trial-specific medications (prednisone, diphenhydramine, famotidine/omeprazole) will be covered once enrolled
L91:     * Calipers will be provided
L92:   * If additional surgery is completed under the same anesthetic event, the client will be financially responsible

L55: Michigan State University Veterinary Medical Center Medical Oncology Service, Microbiology & Molecular Genetics Laboratory, and Precision Health Program
L56: 
L57: Study Title: Efficacy and safety of a novel anti-cancer therapeutic for the treatment of metastatic mammary carcinoma in cats
L58: Purpose of Study: Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade.
L59: The objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel therapeutic targeting miR-10b, a molecule responsible for viability of metastatic cells in cats with mammary carcinoma. This multipurpose therapy has a previously demonstrated efficacy in halting breast cancer invasion and metastasis in mice. The advantage of our novel therapeutic over existing drugs is that it can also be used to visualize primary and metastatic lesions in vivo by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
L60: Studies in cats with mammary carcinoma will help bring this therapeutic into clinic to treat human breast cancer.
L61: Inclusion Criteria (may be evaluated at MSU or at primary care):
L62:   * Histologic or cytologic diagnosis confirmatory of mammary carcinoma with metastasis
L63:   * Diagnosis of metastatic lesions confirmed via cytology/histopathology if accessible, or based on clinical suspicion
L64:   * Non-ulcerated primary/external mammary carcinoma lesions, total volume up to 8 cm^{3}, subject to the overall health evaluation
L65:   * Overall health criteria, adequate liver function, adequate renal function, expected survival >4 weeks
L66:   * Lymph node metastasis, or any other metastatic invasion to be confirmed by cytology and/or CT scan
L67:   * Cases that have not undergone surgery or have undergone unilateral or bilateral mastectomy with metastatic involvement will be included
L68:   * Tumors with or without prior chemotherapy, concurrent NSAIDs are allowed
L69:   * Confirmed microRNA-10b overexpression > log 2 in lesion vs non-tumor parenchyma
L70:   * Informed client consent signed and willingness to consent to drug administration at multiple intervals, blood draws, return visits, monthly CT scans, post-mortem examination
L71: Study Treatment: Cats with metastatic mammary carcinoma will first undergo a baseline CT scan. Cats will also undergo diagnostic imaging (MRI) before and 24 hours after the injection of the therapeutic to ensure its accumulation in the tumor lesion(s). For all imaging (MRI or CT scan) cats will be maintained under anesthesia using routine anesthesia methods and will be monitored closely by veterinary specialists.
L72: After the first injection, treatment will be repeated in two weeks followed by monthly CT scans and treatments. The follow up period may be extended for up to 12 months after initial treatments based on response.
L73: Compensation: This is a funded study: cats will receive the investigational therapeutic and associated imaging free of cost. Pet owners are financially responsible for all treatments and diagnostics that are unrelated to the study.

L33: # Evaluation of TLR agonist Z-007 in dogs with cancer
L34: 
L35: 【11†< BACK TO ALL CLINICAL-TRIALS】
L36: 
L37:   * Recruiting
L38:   * Dog
L39:   * Oncology
L40: While significant improvements in immune based cancer treatments have been made, stimulating an effective immune response to most cancers remains a challenge. The purpose of this study is to evaluate a new agent called Z-007 that works by stimulating immune cells by binding key proteins called Toll Like Receptors (TLRs). These TLRs are responsible for alerting the immune system and helping to create inflammation, that then activates other cells that are important for killing tumor cells.
L41: Preliminary unpublished studies of Z-007 have demonstrated good activity in mouse models of cancer when Z-007 is given by either intravenous or intratumoral injection. Additionally, a previous study was completed in pet dogs with a variety of cancers to provide preliminary data on safety and effectiveness of Z-007. Of the 7 dogs treated, 3 had greater than 30% shrinkage of their tumors, and another two had unexpectedly long durations of stable disease.
L42: The Z-007 was well tolerated by all dogs, with mild nausea post treatment being the only side effect noted. In the current study, dogs with solid tumors (carcinomas, sarcomas, melanoma) will be treated with Z-007 by either intratumoral or intravenous injection, and we will follow them to determine response to treatment to identify the most effective dose and route for administration.
L43: We will also collect tumor and blood samples to understand how Z-007 alters the local and systemic immune system, with the goal of identifying key biomarkers associated with response to treatment. Together, these studies will provide important data that will help improve the use of Z-007 in dogs with cancer.
L44: ## Inclusion Criteria
L45: Pet dogs will be eligible for enrollment if they have: a solid tumor (carcinoma, sarcoma) between 2-7 cm in size that is amenable to repeat biopsy; no significant underlying co-morbidities (kidney, heart, liver disease); no abnormalities in cell or platelet counts on a complete blood count; no prior treatments with immunotherapy agents; and no history of autoimmune disease.
L46: Dogs may not have received any previous treatment for their cancer, or may have failed standard cancer treatments (surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy). While the presence of metastasis is not an exclusion factor, dogs must have a life expectancy of at least 8 weeks. Dogs must also be at least 7 kg in size.
L47: ## Exclusion Criteria
L48: 
L49:   * Significant underlying heart, kidney or liver disease
L50:   * Tumors less than 2 cm and greater than 7 cm in size will be excluded
L51: ## Client Benefits
L52: 
L53: For participation in the this clinical study, all costs associated with treatment of your dog’s cancer with Z-007 will be covered up to Day 63 of the study. The study will cover treatment for side effects related to the Z-007 administration and biopsy (i.e., vomiting, diarrhea, infection of the biopsy site) but it will not cover treatment of conditions unrelated to the study, such as bladder infection, ear infection, etc.
L54: If you choose to continue the Z-007 after Day 63, you will be responsible for the costs associated with the study visits and routine bloodwork.
L55: ## Sample or Data Requirements
L56: To be eligible for enrollment, your dog must be at least 7 kg in size, have a solid tumor (carcinoma, sarcoma, melanoma) between 2-7 cm in size that can be biopsied and/or have tumor spread (metastasis) to the lungs. Your dog must have no significant kidney, heart, or liver disease and no abnormalities on a complete blood count. Your dog must not have received any prior treatments with immune therapy, and must not have had an autoimmune disease.
L57: Your dog may have been previously treated with surgery, chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy, or may have be untreated for their cancer. Dogs may have not received any previous treatment for their cancer, or may have failed standard cancer treatments (surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy). Baseline screening tests include routine bloodwork (complete blood count, chemistry panel), a urine exam, and chest x-rays.
L58: Once enrolled in the study, your dog will have blood collected for the study (15 mls, approximately 1 tablespoon) and a tumor biopsy will be performed under sedation (this is not general anesthesia). Your dog will then have the Z-007 given by either intravenous or intratumoral injection once per week for 4 weeks (Days 0, 7, 14, 21); on Day 14, study blood will be collected again.
L59: On Day 28 of the study, the routine bloodwork and chest x-rays (if applicable) will be repeated, as well as the study blood collection and a second tumor biopsy. If your dog is doing well with either stable disease or a complete/partial shrinkage of tumor, Z-007 will be administered again on D35 and D49. The routine bloodwork, chest x-rays, study blood collection and tumor biopsy will then be repeated on D63.
L60: If your dog continues to do well, then they may recieve the Z-007 every 2 weeks for up to 6 months on a compassionate use basis. The Study Calendar on the last page of this consent provides an overview of all the required study visit and associated study activities.

L0@P0: Funded Study: Canine oral malignant melanoma
L1@P0: Study Title: Evaluating CD 45-binding interleukin-12 and interleukin-15 fusion peptide
L2@P0: in tumor bearing dogs.
L3@P0: Purpose of Study/Background/Objectives: We will be evaluating the safety and
L4@P0: immune activating effects of injecting the combination of IL-12/IL-15 fusion peptide into
L5@P0: oral melanoma tumors after one dose of radiation therapy. IL-12 and IL-15 have
L6@P0: separately been shown to work reasonably well to stimulate the immune system against
L7@P0: canine melanoma and safety has been proven in mice. Previous trials in pet dogs with
L8@P0: IL-12 have been successful. In this trial, canine patients with oral melanoma will be
L9@P0: evaluated to determine if administration of the IL12/IL-15 fusion protein can exert clinical
L10@P0: benefit.
L11@P0: Inclusion Criteria:
L12@P0: • Dogs at least 1 yr old and 8kgs
L13@P0: • Confirmed oral melanoma by cytology or histopathology
L14@P0: • Tumors must be 1-5 cm in diameter
L15@P0: • No previous radiation, chemotherapy or immunotherapy.
L16@P0: • While on study, no immunosuppressive/homeopathic/alternative therapy
L17@P0: including prednisone, cyclosporine or other immune modulatory agents.
L18@P0: • Adequate organ function for sedation and contrast
L19@P0: Exclusion Criteria
L20@P0: • Previous radiation, chemotherapy or immunotherapy
L21@P0: Eligibility Diagnostics: (Within 28 days of starting therapy)
L22@P0: • CBC, Chemistry panel, U/A
L23@P0: • Confirmation of oral melanoma by cytology or histopathology.
L24@P0: • Cytology of the draining lymph node
L25@P0: Treatment/Protocol:
L26@P0: Patients will receive 1 dose of radiation therapy and then 4 doses of IL-12/IL-15
L27@P0: intratumorally. Injections are given 2 weeks in a row, with a 3-week break, then 2
L28@P0: additional weeks of treatment. • At each treatment, blood samples will be collected over
L29@P0-1: 24hrs. Patients can either stay in hospital or return the next day for a blood draw. • After treatment, rechecks will be once every 4 weeks for 3 visits, then once every 8 weeks for
L30@P1: 3 visits, then every 12 weeks for a total of 1.5yrs, then study is complete. • We will use
L31@P1: complete bloodwork, lymph nodes samples, CT scans and biopsies of the tumor to track
L32@P1: patients’ response.
L33@P1: Owner Commitments:
L34@P1: • You are responsible for the initial exam and diagnostics to determine eligibility
L35@P1: • You are expected to make and keep all appointments associated with the study
L36@P1: • You are responsible for all costs associated with unrelated medical conditions
L37@P1: Compensation: This is a fully funded trial once your pet is deemed eligible

L13: # 【5†Con fármaco la UNAM busca curar el cancer en perros y gatos】
L14: 
L15: El uso experimental del fármaco en perros y gatos, además de ofrecer una expectativa de vida a las mascotas, reduce la brecha para alcanzar la aplicación en humanos
L16: 
L17: Nicté Madrigal
L18: 
L19: Hace 7 meses
L20: 
L21: 162649
L22: 
L23: 【6†Image】
L24: 
L25: Un tratamiento contra el cáncer ya se aplica de forma experimental en perros y gatos, como antesala a los ensayos en humanos. - Foto: Cortesía.
L26: 
L27: 【7†Ensenada, B.C.】
L28: Un equipo de investigadores de la UNAM ha desarrollado un fármaco a base de nanopartículas de plata con el que se busca transformar el tratamiento oncológico.
L29: 
L30: La innovación, que ya cuenta con registro de patente, destaca por su capacidad para combatir tumores sin los efectos secundarios de las quimioterapias convencionales, actuando además como un agente genoprotector.
L31: 
L32: Actualmente en fase experimental, el fármaco se ha convertido en una alternativa de vida para perros y gatos.
L33: Los resultados positivos en pacientes veterinarios no solo ofrecen esperanza a los dueños o tutores de mascotas, sino que aceleran el camino para que esta nanotecnología pueda ser aplicada próximamente en humanos.
L34: El proyecto con clave CBF-2025-G-82, liderado por la Dra. Nina Bogdanchikova, que forma parte de la convocatoria de Ciencia Básica y de Frontera de la La Secretaría de Ciencia, Humanidades, Tecnología e Innovación (Secihti), podría constituir uno de los avances más sólidos de la nanomedicina, uniendo la precisión científica con un enfoque ético y humano.
L35: La investigadora expuso que Proyecto del SECIHTI CBF-2025-G-82 “Ruptura del paradigma actual en Nanomedicina”, es una combinación farmacéutica que reduce el daño en el ADN de las células y el daño o destrucción de células (daño cito y genotóxico) de agentes quimioterapéuticos.
L36: 
L37: La patente fue otorgada el 23 enero de 2026, y sus titulares son la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM), la Universidad Autónoma de Baja California (UABC), y la Universidad Autónoma de Guadalajara (UAG).
L38: La doctora Bogdanchikova indicó que una vez que el Secihti asignó recursos al proyecto, estudiaron la posibilidad de aplicar nanopartículas de plata - desarrolladas en conjunto con científicos rusos- para tratar el cáncer.
L39: 
L40: “Nosotros hicimos experimentos in vitro y también en vivo (en ratones). Descubrimos que la aplicación de nanopartículas de plata contenidas en una sustancia desarrollada en la UNAM, arrojó resultados positivos en los ratones.
L41: A partir de esta fase, procedimos a trabajar en una etapa intermedia con perros y gatos, ya que esto representa un escalón más para avanzar en la realización de estudios clínicos con humanos”, explicó.
L42: 
L43: Puntualizó que se trata de nanopartículas de plata especiales, ya que tienen propiedades diferentes a otras.
L44: “Hay muchos grupos que preparan diferentes formulaciones de nanopartículas de plata. Nosotros obtuvimos una patente porque descubrimos que nuestras nanopartículas de plata no son genotóxicas. Esto significa que no hay mutación de órganos al momento de utilizarlas. Esa es la diferencia con otras nanopartículas de plata que existen en el mundo”, detalló.
L45: La investigadora compartió que, otra propiedad, es que estas nanopartículas de plata pueden prevenir la genotoxicidad de otros fármacos por su propiedad genoprotectora.
L46: 
L47: “Con esta patente se abre la ruta para curar el cáncer con partículas que no hacen daño al organismo”, destacó.
L48: 
L49: 
L50: 
L51: Tu mascota puede ser candidata a recibir el tratamiento
L52: Norma Elvia Díaz Ramos, egresada de la licenciatura en Medicina Veterinaria y Zootecnia de la UPAEP, y colaboradora en el proyecto, comentó que en esta fase experimental trabajan en estrecha colaboración con el Hospital Veterinario Peña Jasso.
L53: 
L54: Indicó que, a la fecha, han brindado atención a 16 pacientes, entre perros y gatos.
L55: “La función de estas nanopartículas de plata es generar la destrucción específica de las células malignas sin dañar el tejido sano. Esto permite que el organismo continúe regenerándose y combatiendo la enfermedad; no lo deprime, al contrario, lo fortalece”, abundó.
L56: 
L57: Se trata, explicó, de un proceso de muerte celular programada (apoptosis); lo contrario es la necrosis.
L58: Reiteró que este fármaco no es genotóxico, brinda un efecto genoprotector y selectividad tumoral, —lo cual ha sido demostrado en estudios in vivo e in vitro—, validando así su aplicación segura en pequeñas especies.
L59: “En mi tesis lo defino como un estudio traslacional, ya que, al igual que en humanos, el cáncer se ha convertido en una de las principales causas de muerte en perros y gatos; en los países desarrollados, es la principal causa de muerte en perros adultos. Aproximadamente 1 de cada 3 perros desarrollará cáncer a lo largo de su vida” detalló.
L60: 
L61: La médico veterinaria mencionó que en cada paciente candidato se analizan diversos factores y variables de su historia clínica.

L110: # Current Clinical Trials
L111: We are currently seeking patients for enrollment in funded oncology clinical trials. Study goals and suitability for each patient are discussed in detail with the clients prior to enrollment.
L112: Although clinical trial enrollment may not be the best option for all patients, in many cases, clinical trial participation provides the opportunity to receive novel, cutting-edge therapies free of charge or at a reduced cost and may facilitate treatment of pets where it would not otherwise be possible due to financial constraints or lack of other therapy options. Criteria for enrollment are outlined for each tumor type below.
L113: Please direct referrals or questions to the Oncology Clinical Trials Service at 573-882-7821.
L114: Current Trials and Studies
L115: 
L116: Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (BI705564) for Canine B‑Cell Lymphoma
L117: 
L118: The University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center is enrolling dogs in a clinical trial evaluating an investigational oral Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) inhibitor—BI705564—for the treatment of newly diagnosed B‑cell lymphoma. This exploratory, multicenter field study aims to assess both efficacy and safety of BTK inhibition in canine patients.
L119: 
L120: Eligibility includes:
L121:   * Dogs >1 year old and 10–50 kg in body weight
L122:   * Naïve, untreated B‑cell lymphoma confirmed by cytology or histology with immunophenotyping (flow cytometry)
L123:   * At least two peripheral lymph nodes ≥2 cm in longest diameter
L124:   * WHO stage II, III, or IV B‑cell lymphoma
L125:   * Adequate organ function on bloodwork and urinalysis
L126:   * Performance score of 0–1 (normal to mildly decreased activity) and life expectancy ≥1 month
L127:   * Owner consent
L128: 
L129: Key exclusions:
L130:   * T‑cell lymphoma or involvement of skin, GI tract, or nervous system
L131:   * Internal‑only disease (mediastinum, liver, spleen) without peripheral lymph node enlargement
L132:   * Prior lymphoma treatment (chemotherapy, Tanovea, Laverdia, radiation) or long‑term corticosteroids (>2 weeks)
L133:   * Hypercalcemia, MDR1 deficiency, pregnancy/lactation, or concurrent trial enrollment
L134: 
L135: Study overview:
L136: Dogs will receive oral BI705564 once daily for 3 months (84 days) at 5 mg/kg, with possible dose escalation to 10 mg/kg in certain cases depending on early target occupancy results.
L137: 
L138: The study includes scheduled evaluations such as:
L139: 
L140:   * Physical examinations and lymph node measurements
L141:   * Quality‑of‑life assessments
L142:   * Bloodwork (CBC, chemistry, lymphoma testing)
L143:   * Lymph node aspirates for target occupancy evaluation
L144:   * Thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound at screening
L145: Follow‑up continues regularly throughout the 12‑week treatment period.
L146: 
L147: Potential benefits:
L148: 
L149:   * Access to a novel investigational BTK inhibitor designed to target B‑cell lymphoma
L150:   * All study‑related diagnostics, monitoring, and investigational drug costs are covered
L151:   * Opportunity to contribute to advancement of veterinary oncology and comparative cancer therapeutics
L152: 
L153: Potential risks:
L154:   * Possible drug‑related side effects (as with any investigational therapy)
L155:   * Risks associated with repeated lymph node aspirates, blood draws, and imaging procedures
L156:   * Dogs may be withdrawn if adverse events occur or if continued participation is not in the animal’s best interest
L157: 
L158: Owner commitment:
L159: 
L160: Owners must agree to:
L161:   * Bring their dog for all required study visits over 12 weeks
L162:   * Administer oral medication daily as directed
L163:   * Allow required diagnostic sampling (bloodwork, lymph node aspirates, imaging)
L164:   * Participate in quality‑of‑life assessments
L165: 
L166: Dogs may be withdrawn at any time. If a dog passes away during the study, postmortem evaluation is requested to improve understanding of treatment effects.
L167: 
L168: Contact
L169: For more information on this study please contact:
L170: 📧 cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu
L171: Please include the subject line: BI705564 BTK Inhibitor Trial
L172: 
L173: COTC033: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers
L174: The University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the safety and effectiveness of a new immunotherapy, the Vaccine Peptide Library (VPL), when given to dogs with cancer. Studies in dogs with cancer will complement current human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent.
L175: 
L176: Criteria:
L177:   * Body weight between 15 and 60 kg
L178:   * Tumor biopsy or cytology to confirm diagnosis
L179:   * Solid tumor measuring 2 to 8 cm
L180:   * No mast cell tumors, cutaneous hemangiosarcomas, thyroid carcinomas, or lymphomas
L181:   * Must not have received ANY prior experimental therapy
L182:   * No concurrent chemotherapy or radiation therapy – 2 week washout period required
L183:   * No concurrent immunomodulatory therapy (including Apoquel or Cytopoint) – 6 week washout period required
L184:   * No concurrent corticosteroids – 1 week washout period required
L185:   * No hypercalcemia causing illness
L186:   * No significant co-morbid illness, which includes, but is not limited to: pulmonary metastatic disease, renal or hepatic failure, history of congestive heart failure or clinical coagulopathy, autoimmune disorders, or uncontrolled endocrinopathies
L187: Benefit:
L188: 
L189:   * Complete cost of all treatments and rechecks covered by study, include initial staging or adverse side effects.
L190:   * This trial is being conducted concurrently with human trials.
L191:   * Contribute to development of an important cancer therapy.
L192:   * At the conclusion of the study, there will be a $1000 monetary gift provided towards additional treatment for your pet’s cancer.
L193: 
L194: To Participate:
L195:   * Pet owners must be willing to transport their dog to and from the treatment center in Columbia, MO for every visit abiding by specific timelines.
L196:   * A full screening will be performed prior to full study enrollment.
L197:   * Participation will require a total of up to 13 weekly visits.
L198: 
L199: For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest 【70†or fill out a short survey here.†missouri.qualtrics.com】
L200: Feline GI Lymphoma Radiation + Chemotherapy
L201: 
L202: The University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of whole abdomen radiation therapy (WART) followed by a chemotherapy protocol (COP/Dox) in cats with spontaneous large cell GI lymphoma.  This study will seek to better understand the effects of radiation therapy prior to receiving chemotherapy for this common feline cancer.
L203: 
L204: Criteria:
L205:   * Feline patients with high grade lymphoma in the GI tract
L206:   * Patients must have cytologically or histopathologically confirmed lymphoma
L207:   * Patients must not have been previously treated with chemotherapy
L208:   * Patients cannot be FeLV or FIV positive or have severe systemic disease that would place them at higher risk with general anesthesia.
L209:   * Patients CANNOT have evidence of lymphoma outside of the abdomen.
L210:   * Eligibility is at the discretion of the investigator.
L211: 
L212: Benefit:
L213:   * The cost of the radiation portion of care (WART) will be covered by the study.
L214:   * Your pet will contribute to development of an important cancer therapy.
L215:   * Patient will receive $1,000 stipend for use at the VHC after completion of radiation therapy
L216: 
L217: To Participate:
L218:   * Pet owners must be willing to transport their cat to and from the treatment center in Columbia, Missouri, for every visit abiding by specific timelines.
L219:   * A full screening including a CBC (complete blood count), serum biochemistry panel, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs (x-rays), and abdominal ultrasound will be performed prior to full study enrollment.
L220:   * Participation will require pets to come to our clinic weekly for a minimum of eight weeks and then every 3 weeks for 5 additional visits, with radiation administered the first week only.
L221: For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest.
L222: 
L223: Gilvetmab for the Treatment of Primary Pulmonary Carcinoma in Dogs
L224: 
L225: The University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the effectiveness of Gilvetmab, an anti-PD1 monoclonal antibody, as a treatment for canine pulmonary carcinoma. Similar treatments have been shown to improve survival in human lung cancer patients.
L226: Criteria:
L227: 
L228:   * Dogs with gross disease and those with microscopic disease
L229:   * No immune-mediated disease or other severe comorbidities
L230:   * No concurrent use of steroids or other immunosuppressive drugs
L231: 
L232: Study Involvement:
L233: 
L234:   * Gilvetmab is given as a slow infusion every two weeks for up to 10 doses.
L235:   * CBC, chemistry, and urinalysis are performed every 4 weeks.
L236:   * Chest x-rays are performed every 8 weeks.
L237: 
L238: Benefit:
L239:   * The study covers the cost of Gilvetmab treatment (ranges from $540 – $1350 per treatment, depending on patient size).
L240:   * Owner is responsive for recheck exams, bloodwork, and x-rays.
L241: 
L242: To Participate:
L243: 
L244:   * Pet owners must be willing to transport their dog to and from the treatment center in Columbia, MO for every visit abiding by specific timelines.
L245:   * A full screening will be performed prior to full study enrollment.
L246:   * Participation will require a total of up to 10 biweekly visits.
L247: For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest 【71†or fill out a short survey here.†missouri.qualtrics.com】
L248: 
L249: LEAH xCAR-T: Canine B-Cell Lymphoma
L250: The University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of lymphodepleting chemotherapy and xenogenic CAR-T cell therapy in dogs with spontaneous CD20+ lymphoma. CAR-T cells are lymphocytes (immune cells) that have had a series of genes added to them that make them professional killers of any cell carrying the target molecule.
L251: This study will seek to better understand the effects of the CAR-T cells on the tumor as well as the dog’s immune system.
L252: Criteria:
L253: 
L254:   * Canine patients weighing over 10kg
L255: 
L256:   * Patients with naive (newly diagnosed) and relapsed (pre-treated) Large Cell B-Cell lymphoma.
L257: 
L258:   * Must be feeling clinically WELL at home.
L259: 
L260:   * Must meet bloodwork requirements and have no evidence of primary gastrointestinal or lung involvement; eligibility is at the discretion of the investigator.

L30: ## Why enroll your dog in a clinical trial?
L31: 
L32: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor of dogs. Nearly 10,000 dogs are diagnosed with this cancer each year.  The incidence of 【8†osteosarcoma in dogs†www.csuanimalcancercenter.org】 is anywhere from 10-50x higher than in humans.  Research in dogs will one day mean better treatment for kids.
L33: Enrolling a dog in a clinical trial can offer several potential benefits to both the individual pet and the broader veterinary community. Here are some reasons why pet owners may consider enrolling their dogs in clinical trials:
L34:   * Access to Cutting-Edge Treatments: Clinical trials often investigate novel treatments, therapies, or medications that are not yet available to the general public. By participating in a clinical trial, pet owners may gain access to potentially more effective or advanced treatments for their dog's condition.
L35:   * Contributing to Scientific Knowledge: Clinical trials are essential for advancing veterinary medicine. By participating, pet owners help researchers gather data and evidence that can lead to new understandings of diseases, improved treatments, and better overall care for animals in the future.
L36:   * Expert Monitoring and Care: Dogs enrolled in clinical trials receive close monitoring and care from experienced veterinarians and researchers. This regular attention can be beneficial in managing the dog's health and detecting any changes or side effects early on.
L37:   * Potential Cost Savings: In some cases, the cost of participating in a clinical trial may be partially or fully covered by the sponsoring organization. This can ease the financial burden on pet owners, especially when dealing with expensive medical treatments.
L38: 
L39:   * Supportive Community: Pet owners in clinical trials become part of a supportive community of other caregivers and veterinary professionals who are invested in finding solutions and improving the health outcomes for animals.
L40:   * Personal Satisfaction: Knowing that they are actively contributing to the advancement of veterinary medicine and potentially helping other animals in the future can be personally rewarding for pet owners.
L41: Before enrolling a dog in a clinical trial, it's crucial for pet owners to thoroughly understand the study's purpose, potential risks, and benefits. They should also discuss the decision with their primary veterinarian to ensure it aligns with their dog's specific health needs and well-being. Clinical trials typically have specific inclusion and exclusion criteria, so not all dogs will be eligible for every study.
L42: Therefore, it's essential to work closely with the research team to determine the most suitable options for the dog's condition.

L33:   * 臨床研究について
L34: ### 臨床研究に対する当院のスタンス
L35: 
L36: 当院は臨床、研究、教育の３本柱により獣医臨床の発展に寄与することを目的とし活動を行なっています。その中で、動物のQOLを尊重した臨床研究により腫瘍に対する新しい治療法を開発し、国内の獣医臨床の発展に寄与することも柱の一つと捉え、動物の生命を尊重しつつ、倫理性、科学性を担保する研究を遂行していきたいと努力しております。
L37: 
L38: ### 臨床研究
L39: 
L40: 臨床研究とは、基礎研究で有効性が期待される薬剤の臨床応用を目的に実施する試験の総称です。試験の信頼性、動物に対する倫理性を担保するために厚生労働省により定められた省令「GCP省令」を遵守する厳格な治験や、試験実施機関に設置された倫理委員会の審査を経て、動物に対する倫理が保たれた臨床研究を実施しています。
L41: 
L42: ### 臨床研究の流れ
L43: 
L44: 臨床研究をご希望される場合、以下の流れとなります。
L45: ・紹介動物病院から当院への紹介
L46: ・適応か否かの判断
L47: ・適応の場合研究に組み入れ。治験実施機関が当院ではない場合、実施機関への紹介
L48: ### 現在行なっている臨床研究
L49: 
L50: 犬の鼻腔内腺癌に対する新規放射線治療
L51: 研究実施機関：麻布大学、日本大学
L52: 
L53: 犬のびまん性大細胞性B細胞性リンパ腫に対する新規治療
L54: （現在受け入れ休止中です）
L55: 研究実施機関：JVCOG（実施機関である東京大学で受診していただきます）
L56: 
L57: 現在行なっている臨床研究について、興味をお持ちになった場合、各研究担当者までご連絡（電話またはメール）ください。
L58: ### 日本獣医がん臨床研究グループ
L59: 
L60: 腫瘍科では、一般社団法人日本獣医がん臨床研究グループ（Japan Veterinary Co-operative Oncology Group: JVCOG）（https://www.jvcog.jp）のメンバーとしてさまざまな臨床研究を行なっています。JVCOGでは、獣医臨床腫瘍学に関連した新薬承認試験や、多施設間臨床試験によって有効性の高い治療法を開発し、がんに罹患した動物の診療の質と治療成績の向上を図ることを目的としています。日本における獣医臨床腫瘍学に関する各分野のオピニオンリーダーが集まり、研究を遂行しております。当院で実施している臨床研究のみならず、さまざまな機関での臨床研究について情報を共有し、最適な治療法をご提案できればと考えております。
